name: Captain Flint and Treasure
description: Captain Fint is involved in another treasure hunt, but have found only one strange problem. The problem may be connected to the treasure's location or may not. That's why captain Flint decided to leave the solving the problem to his crew and offered an absurdly high reward: one day off. The problem itself sounds like this... There are two arrays $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ of length $$$n$$$. Initially, an $$$ans$$$ is equal to $$$0$$$ and the following operation is defined: Choose position $$$i$$$ ($$$1 \le i \le n$$$); Add $$$a_i$$$ to $$$ans$$$; If $$$b_i \neq -1$$$ then add $$$a_i$$$ to $$$a_{b_i}$$$. What is the maximum $$$ans$$$ you can get by performing the operation on each $$$i$$$ ($$$1 \le i \le n$$$) exactly once ? Uncle Bogdan is eager to get the reward, so he is asking your help to find the optimal order of positions to perform the operation on them.
input_specification: The first line contains the integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the length of arrays $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$. The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$−10^6 \le a_i \le 10^6$$$). The third line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n$$$ ($$$1 \le b_i \le n$$$ or $$$b_i = -1$$$). Additional constraint: it's guaranteed that for any $$$i$$$ ($$$1 \le i \le n$$$) the sequence $$$b_i, b_{b_i}, b_{b_{b_i}}, \ldots$$$ is not cyclic, in other words it will always end with $$$-1$$$.
output_specification: In the first line, print the maximum $$$ans$$$ you can get. In the second line, print the order of operations: $$$n$$$ different integers $$$p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$$$ ($$$1 \le p_i \le n$$$). The $$$p_i$$$ is the position which should be chosen at the $$$i$$$-th step. If there are multiple orders, print any of them.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1388D — Captain Flint and Treasure [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
